world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: In the majority of Australian languages word stress (or accent) falls on the first syllable, but there are exceptions, one of them being Mathi-Mathi, where the stress in words of more than two syllables falls on various syllables according to certain principles (Hercus 1986d:115). Tyers marks stress and it appears that stress falls regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words, of which there are numerous examples. [p. 29:] karrìp thigh / bebì father / werìte banksia / kannòc waddy / There are a few examples of longer words with stress marked variously. Lindsay also marks stress. In his notation, stress on disyllabic words is predominantly on the second syllable. As with Tyers, stress on longer words appears on various syllables.
new_statements.citation: Blake, Barry J. 2003. The Warrnambool Language: A consolidated account of the Aboriginal language of the Warrnambool area of the Western District of Victoria based on nineteenth-century sources. Pacific Linguistics 544. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blake's consolidated grammar (the only modern description) has no speaker data; it reports that two 19th-century recorders (Tyers 1878, Lindsay 1892) marked stress on the final/second syllable of disyllables and inconsistently on longer words, and he notes this departs from the usual Australian initial-stress pattern. Hercus 1986:159-160, the one source with phonetic notes from an actual (last) speaker, transcribes every 2-3-syllable word with initial stress ([ˈθammɔn], [ˈkurəmUk], [ˈŋammatjItj], [ˈmalaŋ]...) and refers to gemination after 'the accented vowel' (first syllable). Taken together: final stress in disyllables per 19th-century orthographies vs initial stress per 1962-3 phonetic notes — no settled rule; if the catalog must pick one, Blake's own reading is 'final in disyllables, variable in longer words' (closest fixed-list label fixed-final, but Blake hedges with 'it appears').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Blake; Hercus gives no secondary marks for Gundidj (her 'secondary stress' remarks in the same volume concern other languages).
new_statements.exceptions: Blake: words of more than two syllables have stress 'marked variously' / 'on various syllables' in both Tyers and Lindsay; Lindsay's disyllables only 'predominantly' second-syllable. Hercus's initial-stress transcriptions from Mr Alberts conflict with the 19th-century marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from 19th-century vocabularies (Tyers' Glenelg/Wannon area list, Lindsay's Lake Condah notes); Hercus's fragments are isolated words from Lake Condah dialect. Note Blake §1.4.3: almost all nouns are consonant-final (historical loss of final vowels), which may bear on the second-syllable marks in disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Blake 2003 covers the whole Warrnambool language (dialects Kuurn Kopan Noot, Peek Whurrong, Wuluwurrung, Pikwurrung, etc.; Mathews' 'Dhauhurtwurru'); the stress marks come from Tyers (Glenelg/Wannon area, western dialects) and Lindsay (Lake Condah). Hercus 1986 §6.1 'Gundidj' = Lake Condah dialect fragments from Mr Angus Alberts, 1962-3. Language name in Glottolog is 'Warrnambool' (warr1257); community name Gunditjmara / Dhauwurd Wurrung / Keerraywoorroong. The scan's named source (Blake 2003 §2.3.6) was retrieved from the ANU Open Research repository (handle 1885/146713), not sealang.

sources.quote: In the majority of Australian languages word stress (or accent) falls on the first syllable, but there are exceptions, one of them being Mathi-Mathi, where the stress in words of more than two syllables falls on various syllables according to certain principles (Hercus 1986d:115). sources.note: Sec. 2.3.6 'Stress', pp. 28-29: based on 19th-century recorders' stress marks — Tyers (1878): stress 'regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words' (karrìp 'thigh', bebì 'father', werìte 'banksia', kannòc 'waddy'), longer words marked variously; Lindsay (1892): disyllables predominantly second-syllable, longer words on various syllables. Blake contrasts this with the usual Australian initial-stress pattern; no modern speaker data.

sources.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian languages: a late survey. Pacific Linguistics B-77. Canberra: ANU. Ch. 6.1 'Gundidj' (phonetic notes on Mr Angus Alberts, Lake Condah, recorded 1962-3), pp. 159-160.
sources.note: No explicit stress rule ('only tentative remarks can be made on the phonetics'), but every phonetic transcription from the last rememberer carries an initial stress mark: [ˈθammɔn] 'meat', [ˈtammerI] 'sheep', [ˈŋammatjItj] 'white man', [ˈkurəmUk] 'possum', [ˈbembai] 'bread', [ˈmoe] 'black duck', [ˈmalaŋ] 'girl', [ˈdelaŋ] 'stringy-bark'; text refers to intervocalic m being geminated 'when it followed the accented vowel' and not 'after an unaccented vowel' (guremug). Implies initial accent in the Lake Condah fragments — contradicting the 19th-century final-stress marks Blake reports.

sources.citation: Mathews, R. H. 1904. The native tribes of Victoria: their languages and customs. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 43(175): 54-70 ('The Dhauhurtwurru grammar', pp. 57ff).
sources.note: Orthography section (p. 56) covers letters, vowel length marks and consonant values only; no statement about accent or stress anywhere in the paper (grep for accent/stress/emphas: none).

sources.citation: Dawson, James. 1881. Australian Aborigines: the languages and customs of several tribes of Aborigines in the Western District of Victoria, Australia. Melbourne: George Robertson.
sources.note: Introductory Note: English orthographic rules 'have been necessarily laid aside, together with the signs of accentuation. Double consonants are used to express emphasis, and double vowels to express prolongation of the sound' — i.e. the main 19th-century source deliberately marks no stress; no rule stated.
